subtype: Snapped at by a stressed teenager [Receiver]
passage:
Dear Shankar dada,
I'm writing this because when I try to say it, you walk off.
Yesterday I was humming while doing my geometry, and you shouted, "Shut up! Can't you ever stop?" so loudly that Maa came running. I didn't know what I'd done. I felt about five years old.
Later Maa told me your physics exam went badly. I get it now. I'd be upset too.
But understanding why doesn't make it okay. I was only humming. I'd like you to say sorry, and next time just tell me you've had a bad day. I'll give you space.
Your brother,
Madhav

qa.q: What was Madhav doing when Shankar shouted?
qa.a: Humming while doing geometry.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel after being shouted at?
qa.a: Madhav felt confused and small, "about five years old", because nothing he had done seemed to explain the shouting 😔

qa.q: What did Madhav choose to ask for in the letter?
qa.a: An apology, and for Shankar to say he's had a bad day next time while Madhav gives him space, which holds both understanding and a fair limit.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Shankar may feel embarrassed and a bit guilty, realising his exam anger landed on a little brother who was only humming.

grounding: A younger brother writes to his older brother that knowing about the bad exam does not make being shouted at acceptable.

subtype: Snapped at by a stressed teenager [Receiver]
passage:
"Bidisha, you've been quiet all day."
Yeah. Can I tell you something, Lakshmi? It's small, but it's been sitting in my chest since last night.
Didi came home from her chemistry board exam. I only asked, "How was it?" and she screamed, "Why do you always have to poke your nose in? Get out of my room!" It isn't even her room. It's our room.
I went and sat on the stairs. I kept thinking, what did I do? I felt tiny.
This morning Ma said Didi's paper went really badly, and I understand, sort of. I'd be a wreck too. But I'm still hurt. A bad exam doesn't mean she gets to scream at me.
Do you think I should tell her that?

qa.q: What did Bidisha ask Didi?
qa.a: "How was it?"

qa.q: Why did Bidisha feel tiny on the stairs?
qa.a: Bidisha had only asked a kind question and couldn't see what was wrong, so being screamed at felt confusing and made Bidisha feel small.

qa.q: What would you advise Bidisha to say to Didi?
qa.a: Once things are calm, something like "I'm sorry the exam went badly, but please don't scream at me", which is kind and still honest about the hurt.

qa.q: What might Didi be feeling by the next morning?
qa.a: Didi is probably still upset about the chemistry paper and may also feel bad about screaming, even if she hasn't said so.

grounding: A younger sibling tells a friend about being screamed at by an older sister after her bad exam, understanding the cause but still hurt.

subtype: Snapped at by a stressed teenager [Receiver]
passage:
I'm Salma's cousin, and I was staying with them the week of the Class 12 prelims. On Wednesday her brother Faiz came home after maths and dropped his bag, and when Salma asked if he wanted to play carrom, he yelled, "Are you stupid? Do I look like I want to play?"
Salma didn't answer. She put the striker back in the box very carefully, as if it might break, and went out to the balcony. Her face was blank, but her ears were red.
Later her Ammi explained that Faiz's paper had gone badly. Salma nodded. Then she said, very quietly, "He still shouldn't talk to me like that." I think she was right.
— Kiran

qa.q: What did Salma ask Faiz?
qa.a: If he wanted to play carrom.

qa.q: What does the careful way Salma put the striker back suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests Salma felt shaken and small, trying not to make things worse after a shout she didn't understand.

qa.q: What could Faiz do once his exam upset settles?
qa.a: Faiz could apologise to Salma, and next time say he's had a bad day and needs space instead of taking it out on her.

qa.q: How does Kiran seem to judge what happened?
qa.a: Kiran understands why Faiz snapped but agrees with Salma that a bad paper didn't make his harshness okay.

grounding: A cousin sees a younger sister shouted at by her brother after his bad prelim, and her quiet point that the cause does not excuse it.

subtype: Snapped at by a stressed teenager [Receiver]
passage:
Monday. Mridul came home from his physics board exam and dropped his bag in the hall. Eshaan, thirteen, only asked, "Can I borrow your charger?" Mridul exploded. "Can't you leave me alone for ONE minute?" Eshaan went into the bathroom and ran the tap so nobody would hear him sniff. What did I even do?
Wednesday. Eshaan kept to the balcony. Maa told him quietly that the physics paper had gone badly and Mridul was scared about his marks. So it wasn't really about the charger, Eshaan thought. That helped a bit. It didn't make the shout feel okay.
Saturday. Mridul knocked on his door. "Sorry about Monday. Bad exam." Eshaan nodded, then made himself say it. "I get that. But you still can't yell at me like that."
Mridul looked at the floor. "Fair."

qa.q: What did Eshaan ask Mridul on Monday?
qa.a: Eshaan only asked, "Can I borrow your charger?"

qa.q: How was Eshaan feeling in the bathroom on Monday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Eshaan felt confused and small 😔; he ran the tap to hide his sniffing and kept asking himself what he had even done.

qa.q: What choice did Eshaan make on Saturday that mattered?
qa.a: Eshaan accepted the apology and the reason but still said the yelling was not okay, rather than letting it pass just because the exam went badly.

qa.q: What might Mridul realise when Eshaan says, "But you still can't yell at me like that"?
qa.a: Mridul may see that Eshaan understood the bad exam and was still hurt, and that the fear about marks was Mridul's to handle, not something to pour onto a younger brother.

grounding: Shows a younger brother shouted at after an older sibling's bad exam, feeling confused and small, and learning that the cause does not excuse the shout.

subtype: Snapped at by a stressed teenager [Receiver]
passage:
"Leave the cup, Jatin, sit. You've been rubbing your eyes since your sister shouted at you. Your Ramesh dada knows that face.
When I was fourteen, in Jabalpur, my sister Kusum sat her matric exams. One evening she came home from the maths paper, and I asked her to come fly kites. She screamed at me, 'Is that all you think about? Useless boy!' I hid behind the water tank on the roof and cried where no one could see. I kept thinking I had done something terrible.
My mother found me there. She said Kusum's paper had gone very badly. Then she said something I have kept for sixty years: 'Her fear is real. Shouting at you is still not right. I will tell her so.'
And she did. Kusum climbed up to the roof later with two kites."

qa.q: Where did young Ramesh hide after Kusum screamed at him?
qa.a: He hid behind the water tank on the roof and cried where no one could see.

qa.q: What did young Ramesh believe while hiding on the roof?
qa.a: He believed he had done something terrible, because the shout came from nowhere and he could not see its real cause; that confusion left him feeling small.

qa.q: Which choice by Ramesh's mother made the difference?
qa.a: She explained Kusum's bad paper but still said the shouting was not right and promised to tell Kusum so, giving both understanding and a clear limit.

qa.q: How might Kusum have seen things when she climbed up to the roof with two kites?
qa.a: Once her fear had cooled and her mother spoke to her, Kusum probably felt sorry; the kites were her way of mending it without many words.

grounding: Illustrates, through a grandfather's memory, a younger brother shouted at after his sister's bad exam, and a mother showing that understanding the stress does not make the shouting acceptable.
